blocks.content: TCP is built entirely around one promise: whatever you send will arrive, complete and in order, or you will at least be told it failed. That promise is genuinely valuable, but it is not free. Honoring it means setting up a connection before a single byte of real data moves, tracking an acknowledgment for what was sent, and waiting, sometimes for a noticeable stretch, to resend anything that got lost along the way.

For a huge amount of software, that cost is worth paying without a second thought. But for some applications, speed genuinely matters more than perfect reliability, and waiting around for one lost data point to be resent would actually make things worse, not better. UDP is the transport protocol built for exactly that case, and this topic is where you meet it properly.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437068109-141651926.png
1. The Price of a Perfect Guarantee
blocks.text: 1. The Price of a Perfect Guarantee

blocks.content: It helps to unpack exactly where TCP's overhead comes from, because none of it is wasted, it is all in service of that one promise. Before either side can exchange a single piece of real data, they have to shake hands, a short back and forth just to agree the connection is open. After that, every piece of data sent needs its arrival confirmed, and the sender has to hold onto a copy of it until that confirmation comes back.

If confirmation never arrives, TCP has to notice, wait out a timeout, and send the data again. Each one of these steps is doing real, necessary work when correctness is the goal. But each one also adds delay, and for time sensitive data, an old lost value resent a moment later can be worse than useless, it can already be pointless by the time it shows up.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437068110-644008060.png
blocks.alt: The Price of a Perfect Guarantee

blocks.title: Where this sits in the module
blocks.content: The Ports topic that opened this module showed you how a device tells its running programs apart. The TCP Overview topic right before this one showed you what a protocol looks like when it is built entirely around correctness. UDP is what a Transport layer protocol looks like when it deliberately chooses speed instead.
2. UDP, Defined Precisely

UDP, User Datagram Protocol, is a connectionless, unreliable, unordered delivery protocol. Each of those three words is doing precise, specific work, and it is worth being exact about what each one actually means rather than treating them as a vague warning label.

Connectionless means there is no handshake and no setup at all. A sender using UDP simply fires its data the moment it is ready. Unreliable means UDP makes no guarantee that any given piece of data actually arrives, and critically, nothing automatically resends it if it is lost along the way. Unordered means UDP does not guarantee data arrives in the same order it was sent, two datagrams sent one after another can legally arrive the other way round.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437068733-188218318.png
3. The Fire and Forget Model

Put those three properties into motion and you get what is usually called the fire and forget model. A sender using UDP packages its data into a single unit, addressed with a source port and a destination port exactly the way you saw ports work in the earlier topic, and sends that unit straight onto the network.

The moment it is sent, the sender is done. It does not wait for any confirmation that the data actually arrived. There is no handshake beforehand, no acknowledgment afterward, and no automatic retry if something goes wrong in between. Whatever happens to that datagram after it leaves is, as far as UDP itself is concerned, no longer the sender's problem.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437068733-604083306.png

blocks.title: A small but useful naming detail
blocks.content: Back in the encapsulation topic, you saw the Transport layer wrap data into a new unit as it heads down the stack. TCP's version of that unit is specifically called a segment. UDP's version is specifically called a datagram, and that is exactly where the protocol's full name, User Datagram Protocol, comes from.
4. A Deliberate Trade, Not a Flaw
blocks.text: 4. A Deliberate Trade, Not a Flaw

blocks.content: It is tempting to hear connectionless, unreliable, and unordered and assume something has gone wrong with UDP. It has not. For a meaningful slice of real data, an old, late arriving copy is actually worse than no data at all, and that single fact is what makes giving up reliability a genuine, valid design choice rather than a shortcoming.

Think about one dropped frame in a live video call. It is barely noticeable, your eye glosses right over it, and trying to resend that one frame would only add delay to everything that comes after it, making the call feel worse, not better. A position update in a live multiplayer game tells a similar story. If it arrives late, it is already useless, because a newer position is already on its way and will replace it within moments anyway.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437068734-322477456.png
blocks.alt: A Deliberate Trade, Not a Flaw

blocks.title: The radio broadcast picture
blocks.content: UDP behaves a lot like a radio station. The station just transmits continuously, out into the air, whether or not your specific radio picks up every single moment cleanly. It does not pause, and it does not wait for you to confirm you heard something before it keeps going. That is precisely UDP's attitude toward the data it sends.
5. The Real Speed Advantage

None of this trade off would be worth making if UDP were not genuinely, measurably faster, and it is. With no handshake delay and no acknowledgment bookkeeping to maintain, UDP has meaningfully lower latency than TCP, and each individual packet carries less overhead too, since there is far less bookkeeping riding along with the actual data.

This speed is not a minor side benefit, it is the entire reason UDP exists despite giving up reliability. Data sent over UDP can start flowing the instant it is ready, with no round trips spent agreeing to talk first, which is exactly why it is the natural choice whenever every millisecond of delay is felt directly by a person on the other end.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437068734-949737457.png
6. A Minimal Header, By Design

UDP's simplicity is not just a description of its behavior, it is baked directly into how little its header actually carries. A UDP header really only needs four things: a source port, a destination port, a length field, and a checksum. That is enough to get a datagram to the right program on the right device and let the receiver notice if it arrived corrupted.

Compare that to TCP's header, which has to carry everything needed to keep its promise: sequence numbers to track order, acknowledgment numbers to confirm receipt, and window size information to manage the flow of data. TCP's header earns every one of those extra fields, but UDP simply does not need any of them, because it never made the promise those fields exist to support.

7. Where UDP Shows Up in the Real World
blocks.text: 7. Where UDP Shows Up in the Real World

blocks.content: UDP is not a niche choice, it quietly powers a surprising amount of the internet you use every day, almost always in situations where staying current matters more than catching every last byte. A handful of concrete examples make the pattern obvious.

Live video and voice calls lean on UDP because a dropped frame passes almost unnoticed, but a delay while TCP waits to resend one lost piece ruins the whole experience for everyone on the call. Online multiplayer games use it because the newest position update always matters more than an old one arriving late. DNS lookups favor UDP's speed too, a lookup is small and quick, and if it fails, the client simply asks again, a story covered in full in its own dedicated module later in this course. Live streaming rounds out the pattern, favoring a steady forward moving stream over pausing to recover every dropped piece.

blocks.content: DNS is one of UDP's biggest real world users, and the full story of how a domain name actually turns into an IP address deserves its own dedicated module later in this course. For now, just recognize that DNS is a natural fit for UDP because each lookup is small and cheaply retried.
8. UDP at a Glance

With TCP and UDP now both properly introduced, it is worth lining their core properties up side by side. This is the table to come back to whenever you are trying to decide which one a piece of software actually needs.

9. Common Mistakes to Avoid

The most common mistake is treating UDP as simply a broken or lesser version of TCP. It is not. It is a deliberate design choice built for a genuinely different set of needs, ones where TCP's guarantees would actively get in the way rather than help. Judging UDP by TCP's goals is judging it by the wrong standard entirely.

A second, closely related mistake is assuming that any application built on UDP never handles reliability at all. That is not true either. Some applications build their own lightweight reliability directly on top of UDP, retrying only the specific pieces they decide actually matter, without paying the cost of TCP's blanket guarantee applied to every single byte.

["UDP is not a worse TCP, it is a deliberate trade of reliability for speed","Connectionless, unreliable, and unordered are precise design choices, not accidents","Some UDP based applications add their own selective reliability where it is actually needed"]
